verses.text: Job again took up his parable, and said,
“Oh that I were as in the months of old, as in the days when God watched over me;
when his lamp shone on my head, and by his light I walked through darkness,
as I was in the ripeness of my days, when the friendship of God was in my tent,
when the Almighty was yet with me, and my children were around me,
when my steps were washed with butter, and the rock poured out streams of oil for me,
when I went out to the city gate, when I prepared my seat in the street.
The young men saw me and hid themselves. The aged rose up and stood.
The princes refrained from talking, and laid their hand on their mouth.
The voice of the nobles was hushed, and their tongue stuck to the roof of their mouth.
For when the ear heard me, then it blessed me; and when the eye saw me, it commended me:
Because I delivered the poor who cried, and the fatherless also, who had no one to help him,
the blessing of him who was ready to perish came on me, and I caused the widow’s heart to sing for joy.
I put on righteousness, and it clothed me. My justice was as a robe and a diadem.
I was eyes to the blind, and feet to the lame.
I was a father to the needy. The cause of him who I didn’t know, I searched out.
I broke the jaws of the unrighteous, and plucked the prey out of his teeth.
Then I said, ‘I shall die in my own house, I shall count my days as the sand.
My root is spread out to the waters. The dew lies all night on my branch.
My glory is fresh in me. My bow is renewed in my hand.’
“Men listened to me, waited, and kept silence for my counsel.
After my words they didn’t speak again. My speech fell on them.
They waited for me as for the rain. Their mouths drank as with the spring rain.
I smiled on them when they had no confidence. They didn’t reject the light of my face.
I chose out their way, and sat as chief. I lived as a king in the army, as one who comforts the mourners.

footnotes.content: Job steps back from the arguments that have worn him thin and speaks from the deepest well of his memory. He begins not with anger but with longing—a shift that opens the door to something more human than his earlier speeches. Sometimes the most honest thing we can say is: I remember when things were different.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Job yearns for the months when God's presence was unmistakable—not hidden, not distant, but felt. That word "watched" carries both protection and intimacy; God was watching *over* him, not watching *for* failure. When our own circumstances grow dark, it helps to remember that the Lord's watching over us has never actually stopped.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A lamp is never its own light—it depends entirely on the one who kindled it. Job speaks of walking through darkness, yet he was never in darkness, because God's lamp shone on his head. The image reminds us that light for our path comes from outside us, and in our darkest seasons, we ask whether that light still shines.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The ripeness of my days"—Job speaks of a season when everything felt full, ready, complete. The friendship of God dwelt in his tent as though He were family. Those seasons do come—not always, but enough to remind us of what the soul longs for: the Lord's company, present and warm.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Job remembers not just God's presence but the wholeness that came with it: the Almighty *with* him, and his children *around* him. Blessing in Scripture often means the simple gift of togetherness—the ones you love near, and the Lord's nearness guarding it all. That vision of home is what suffering strips away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The language shifts to abundance so overflowing it becomes almost comic: steps washed in butter, rocks pouring out oil like water. Job isn't exaggerating—he's speaking the language of plenty, the way a poor man speaks of a feast he once saw. Prosperity in those days meant your fields gave more than you asked for.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The city gate was where power lived—where disputes were settled and the community gathered. That Job "prepared his seat in the street" means he held authority there, respected enough that people came to him. This sets the stage for what follows: his influence came from a reputation earned through justice, not mere wealth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Young men hiding themselves and the aged rising—it's a picture of respect so deep it borders on reverence. Job's presence commanded a room without him having to speak. True influence rests on something more solid than words or rank; it rests on a character people trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The princes laid their hands on their mouths—a gesture of deference, of listening. When someone of Job's standing enters a room, the powerful themselves fall silent. This wasn't arrogance on Job's part; it was the natural effect of a life lived with integrity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The voice of nobles hushed, their tongues stuck—a vivid image of being struck speechless. Job has become a kind of moral authority that silences pride. There's something both beautiful and tragic here: such a man, and now here he sits in sackcloth, arguing with his friends.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Job's reputation preceded him—when people heard of him, they blessed him; when they saw him, they commended him. That kind of renown doesn't come from wealth alone. It comes from a life that has genuinely served others, and people sense the difference.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Job delivered the poor and the fatherless—the ones with no advocate, no one to plead their case. His justice wasn't abstract; it moved his hands to act for the helpless. This is the root of all the respect that preceded him: he used his strength for those who had none.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A widow's heart singing for joy—that simple image says more than any catalog of deeds. The widows and the dying would have had no one; Job became their friend, their deliverer. Their blessing returned to him because what he did came from genuine compassion, not a hunger for praise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Righteousness as a robe, justice as a crown—Job pictures his character as something he wore openly, visibly, like a king's attire. In the ancient Near East, a leader's robe and crown declared who they were and what they stood for. Job's justice was his true garment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eyes to the blind, feet to the lame—Job gave people what they lacked. He became, for those without resources, the one who could see and move on their behalf. To be someone's eyes or feet is to enter their vulnerability, to say: I will help you go where you cannot go alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A father to the needy—Job assumed responsibility for strangers as a father would for his own children. He didn't wait for people to come asking; he "searched out" the cause of those he didn't even know. That kind of proactive justice marks a man whose conscience won't let him rest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Job broke the jaws of the wicked and rescued prey from their teeth—a fierce image of protective justice. He wasn't passive; he actively opposed those who preyed on the weak. Righteousness sometimes requires strength turned against cruelty, on behalf of the defenseless.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Job expected to die peacefully at home, his days as countless as sand—a vision of a long, settled life crowned with honor. He planned for security and rest, the natural hope of a man at peace with himself and his God. How quickly that expectation would shatter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A root spread to the waters, dew lying all night on the branch—Job uses the language of a flourishing tree in a well-watered land. Trees in Scripture often speak of stability and blessing. His roots ran deep; nothing seemed likely to uproot him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Glory fresh, bow renewed—Job expected to remain vigorous, useful, strong. He wasn't aging into decline; his vigor renewed itself like a warrior's bow drawn and strung again. He imagined growing old with honor still intact, still able to serve.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Men listened, waited, kept silence for his counsel—Job's words held weight because they came from wisdom earned through living justly. People didn't just hear him; they truly listened, waiting for his voice. That's the kind of influence that can only be built over years of faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After his words, people didn't speak again—his counsel settled things. When wisdom speaks true, it brings a kind of finality; it satisfies the restless mind. Job's speech "fell on" people, landing like rain on thirsty earth, and that ended the conversation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: People waited for him as they wait for rain, their mouths drinking him in—an image of deep thirst satisfied. Job's wisdom wasn't ornamental; it addressed the deepest needs of those who heard him. In a dry land, a man with wisdom is worth more than gold.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When Job smiled, people took courage. His face had become a source of light and hope to those around him. The light of his face—a phrase that echoes the light of God's countenance—had become a gift he gave to those who were afraid.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in Job's claim: he chose people's way, sat as chief, lived as a king comforting the mourners. He imagined himself settled in that role forever—wise, safe, honored. We know from our own lives how quickly such visions can shatter, and how the Lord meets us in the shattered places.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
